science.description: 5 min read NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy. Watch to learn how the presence of a planet modifies the gravitational wave signal from tightly orbiting white dwarfs. The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory could detect a Jupiter-mass planet in such systems up to thousands of light-years away. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Download high-resolution video from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio “The most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,” said Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “If an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way we’ll be able to uncover.” Two papers published Tuesday in The Astrophysical Journal detail the findings. The first , authored solely by McGrath, examines the detection method and determines the planet masses and orbital periods where it would work best. The second paper , by McGrath and coauthors, investigates how such planets could be confirmed using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope . The possibility of detecting exoplanets around LISA double white dwarf systems was first proposed by Japanese astronomer Naoki Seto in 2008. Led by ESA (European Space Agency), the LISA mission is slated for launch in the mid-2030s. As a collaborative partner, NASA is contributing the telescopes, other critical hardware, and engineering and scientific support as part of its mission to better understand how the universe works. The LISA detection method is similar to one called radial velocity that uses light and is already employed to find exoplanets around nearby stars. As a planet orbits, its gravity tugs on its host star, imparting a small reflex motion, or wobble, onto it. This wobble causes the star’s spectrum to oscillate, with spectral lines shifting from redder wavelengths as the star moves away from us to bluer ones as the star moves toward us. The shift is due to a phenomenon called the Doppler effect . “Something similar occurs with gravitational waves,” said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the confirmation paper. “By themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency. The DARPA-funded project saw a robotic "truss builder" create a reflective antenna using Kapton film, composite fiber tubes and aluminum joints. The implications are huge for future missions, potentially opening up new possibilities to build — or fix — satellites in the final frontier. "This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space ," Sergio Pellegrino, an aerospace and civil engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement on Nov. 5 . The need for such spacecraft will likely rise substantially in the future, as companies assemble giant megaconstellations for cell-phone communications, AI compute and other purposes. Indeed, the ball is already rolling on such ambitious projects, generating enough hype for space startups around the globe to raise a record $20.8 billion in the third quarter of 2026 alone. Anything that launches aboard a rocket is limited by the size of that vehicle's fairing — the nose cone that protects payloads during their ride to space. In space, however, the ability to stretch out is practically infinite — after taking into account, of course, engineering and financing constraints. Assembling structures robotically off Earth could therefore be revolutionary, advocates say. And the recent milestone was a step in that direction. "This work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics, but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power ," said Pellegrino, who's team leader of the truss-building project, a Caltech demonstration mission called Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA). ASTRA built a 1.4-meter-wide (4.5-foot) structure in orbit. "NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," NOM4D Program Manager Andrew Detor said in a Nov. 5 DARPA statement . science.title: Curiosity Mars rover sizes up new 'Nazca' dig site | Space photo of the day for Nov. 10, 2026
science.description: null NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity acquired this close-up image using its Mars Hand Lens Imager, showing the abundance of disc-shaped potential crystal forms on our next drill target, dubbed "Nazca." (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) NASA's Curiosity Mars rover is sizing up its next dig site on the Red Planet. The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of the Mars site, informally named "Nazca," as thoroughly as possible before drilling into it. What is it? Curiosity snapped the close-up image on Oct. 18, 2026, using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). The image shows multiple roughly disk-shaped potential crystal formations at the rover's next drill target. MAHLI is located on the turret at the end of the rover's robotic arm. It uses an onboard focusing process to make a composite of images of the same target acquired at different positions to focus on multiple features in a single image. Why is it incredible? Scientists theorize that the "discs and needles" texture takes its characteristic shape as crystals, or "crystal forms," grow. The relatively large sizes of the crystal forms at "Nazca" may provide clues about the temperatures at which they grew, as well as information about the abundance of salts and fluids in the area at the time. Complicating this picture, however, is the fact that mineral crystals can be replaced by other minerals after their original crystallization. The new minerals are known as "pseudomorphs," because they have the same shape as the original minerals but not the same composition or molecular structure. The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of Nazca — which shares its name with an ancient South American civilization that's famous for the large designs it etched into the rock and dirt — before drilling begins. The NASA researchers will then be able to compare the deeper composition to the surface-level composition.

science.title: What is the electrification target at COP31 and can countries meet it?
science.description: Relying on electricity for more of our energy is vital to efforts to limit global warming Christian Hütter/mauritius images GmbH/Alamy One of the key items being discussed at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, this week is a voluntary global target to increase electricity’s share of total final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035. This 35 by 35 target is based on analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) on what is needed to keep the 1.5°C global warming target within reach. Currently, electricity is estimated to make up just 23.4 per cent of the energy delivered to consumers, known as final energy – a figure that has increased by only 6.7 percentage points since 2000. This means that hitting the target will require the rate of electrification to quadruple compared with the first quarter of the 21st century and triple compared with the rate between 2020 and 2025. Judit Hecke at New Climate Institute, a German think tank, says such an acceleration is possible but “the challenge is getting policies, investment and infrastructure moving at the same pace”. Advertisement Progress on renewable energy has been encouraging, with renewables making up a higher proportion of overall electricity production year after year, and renewable capacity additions have been setting new records each year. In 2024, the most recent IRENA data, nearly 32 per cent of global electricity production came from renewable sources compared with just 18 per cent in 2000. Renewable energy capacity has increased from 0.8 terawatts in 2000 to 5.2 terawatts in 2025. But this is a long way from the COP28 pledge for UN member states to reach 11 terawatts of renewable capacity by 2030. However, Hecke points out that the electrification target includes electricity regardless of how it is generated, meaning that a country could make progress while still heavily relying on coal and gas in the power sector. Electrification, renewables and energy efficiency should be looked at together as the “three pillars of the energy transition”, says Hecke. “At COP31, governments should back the target as part of this wider transition and set out how they will deliver it nationally.” Read more Solar energy is going to power the world much sooner than you think Jan Rosenow at the University of Oxford says the 35 by 35 target is “broadly the right level of ambition” and it is achievable now that electric vehicles , electrical industrial heat and heat pumps are often the cheapest options. “Most new electricity generation built today is renewables and batteries. Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30 , the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras. Not only has Emily been proved right, but perhaps she didn’t go quite far enough. science.title: Total solar eclipse 2027 vs 2028 — Which one should you choose, Egypt or Australia?
science.description: null For those who want to experience a total solar eclipse, the next two years present the best kind of problem. On Aug. 2, 2027, the so-called "eclipse of the century " will sweep across southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, bringing more than six minutes of totality to parts of Egypt. Then, on July 22, 2028, another exceptionally long total solar eclipse will cross Australia, putting the remote Outback and Sydney Harbor in the path of the moon's dark central shadow before it reaches New Zealand's beautiful South Island. Both eclipses will be spectacular, and both will require careful planning, yet they promise very different experiences. The 2027 event combines over six minutes of totality with some of the very best weather prospects possible, while 2028 offers over five minutes of totality above some of the world's most famous wildernesses and cityscapes. Eclipse chasing requires careful planning and dedication, but also significant funds. If you can only choose one, which should it be? 2027 total solar eclipse: pros and cons A map of the 2027 total solar eclipse path. (Image credit: Michael Zeiler/EclipseAtlas.com) On paper, 2027 is difficult to beat. Maximum totality on Aug. 2 will last about 6 minutes, 23 seconds, making it the longest totality on land since 1991 and until 2114. The path of totality will cross southern Spain and Gibraltar before sweeping across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Somalia and the Chagos Islands. About 88.9 million people live in its path, according to Time and Date . It will dominate the news for weeks. For Europeans, southern Spain is the obvious easy option. Tarifa, at the country's southern tip, will see about 4 minutes, 39 seconds of totality, while the U.K. Overseas Territory of Gibraltar gets about 4 minutes, 25 seconds. Travel farther east and the duration increases, with Sfax in Tunisia getting around 5 minutes, 41 seconds and locations in Egypt experiencing more than six minutes. Weather prospects generally improve, too, as the path crosses the deserts of North Africa. Egypt is the headline destination. Luxor will see about 6 minutes, 20 seconds of totality near midday, with Karnak Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the world's greatest ancient monuments nearby. The climatic odds are excellent, with clouds extremely rare in early August. That combination of a very long totality, ancient landscapes and a very high probability of a clear sky makes 2027's path of totality highly unusual. But there are downsides. science.title: NASA's twin ESCAPADE Mars probes slingshot around Earth in unprecedented double 'gravity assist'
science.description: null Twin NASA spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long escapade, ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet. The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) spacecraft launched in November 2025 on the second-ever flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. But rather than head straight to Mars, the two spacecraft dawdled through a looping trajectory . Now, they are back in Earth's neighborhood where they tackled a crucial engine burn unusually close to Earth that — if all goes well — will set them on track for Mars . "No NASA mission has ever done this before," said Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and principal investigator of the ESCAPADE mission. "For most missions, it just isn't necessary." That's because traditionally NASA's Mars missions have been carefully choreographed within cosmic launch constraints, leaving Earth during a brief window of planetary alignment that only occurs every 26 months. ESCAPADE was meant to launch in October 2024, when Earth and Mars were favorably aligned, but delays with the New Glenn rocket forced the mission to sit out the precious launch window. Rather than wait to launch this fall, NASA decided to try something new. ESCAPADE mission planners designed a "loitering" orbit , shaped like a kidney bean. It called for the twin probes to loop through that trajectory to be back at Earth in early November 2026, ready to continue on to Mars. The ESCAPADE mission's unique path to reach Mars. After launching in November 2025, the twin ESCAPADE probes looped around the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 (L2), in a "loiter" orbit that returned them to Earth in November 2026 where they used our planet's gravity to slingshot themselves to Mars. (Image credit: Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger) Once they arrived, however, the twin probes faced a major hurdle: Each had to perfectly execute an engine burn within Earth's gravity well. The maneuver is similar to the slingshot flybys that spacecraft regularly conduct to adjust their trajectories — but here, the probes had to fire their engines to amp up the effect of the burn rather than acting alone. The first spacecraft tackled the feat on Nov. 7; the second did so on Monday (Nov. 9). And according to NASA, the burns went perfectly. "This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we've now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days," Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for NASA's Heliophysics Division said in a statement . Such a Saturn ian eclipse, more formally called an occultation , was visible in early 2025 along a small swath of Earth — from Greenland through central Europe and into northern Africa . The bright dot near Saturn is not a moon of Saturn , but rather the star 85 Aquarii , which is further behind Saturn than Saturn is behind the Moon.
